title: Row-buffer XOR tree: every activation doubles as full-row scrub
idea: Combine the activation path with patrol scrubbing: a hard-wired XOR tree under the sense-amp stripe computes parity over each 1 KB segment of the opened row and compares it with parity bits stored in that row, so every ordinary activate checks the whole 8 KB page rather than only the 64 B fetched. Mismatching segments are flagged to a background corrector before errors accumulate.
why: Retention tail and row hammer (facts 3, 9) and overfetch (fact 8): ~128x more bits checked per activate at no extra activation energy, so refresh can stretch 2-4x because weak-cell flips are caught early.

title: Soft-decision sensing plus NAND LDPC to read tiny capacitors
idea: Combine the DRAM sense amp with NAND flash soft-read: the bitline is compared against 3-7 shifted references (a mini flash-ADC sharing one regenerative latch) to give per-bit confidence, and a short-latency LDPC decoder at the bank uses those log-likelihoods. Cells with roughly half today's charge (~2.5 fF, AR ~35) then read at acceptable error rates.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): halving required Cs cuts capacitor aspect ratio ~2x, saving etch/deposition steps and easing 3D tiers; costs ~6-10% parity and a few ns.

title: Write-hot pages on leaky rows: application writes become free refresh
idea: Combine the OS page allocator with per-row retention profiling: pages whose write interval is shorter than a row's measured retention are placed on weak rows, since every write restores full charge; those rows become refresh-exempt while a write-interval monitor guarantees the deadline, and only cold-data rows get nominal refresh.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): makes the weakest 1-5% of rows usable without remapping and skips their refresh, cutting refresh energy/bandwidth ~10-30% and recovering yield.

title: Elastic twin-cell rows: weak rows fold into differential pairs
idea: Combine the 1T1C array with 2T2C twin-cell sensing, switchable per row: a mode bit in the row decoder makes rows containing weak cells store each bit as a complementary pair on adjacent bitlines, doubling signal and cancelling common-mode leakage at half capacity for those rows only; strong rows stay 1T1C.
why: Retention tail and charge wall (facts 1, 3): trades 50% capacity on the ~1-3% weak rows for ~2x sense margin instead of scrapping dies; allows lower Cs targets.

title: RAID-5 inside the HBM stack ships dies with dead banks
idea: Combine storage RAID with die stacking: the base die stripes each cache line across N data dies plus rotating parity, so a stack with a dead bank or die region still works by reconstruction; known-bad regions are treated as erasures, which doubles correction power versus unknown errors.
why: HBM yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6): turning bad-bank stacks into sellable parts could recover much of that loss, cutting effective HBM cost/bit 10-25%.

title: Erasure-coded TSV lanes replace spare TSVs and repair fuses
idea: Combine network forward-error-correction with the TSV interface: data crosses the stack as Reed-Solomon codewords spread over all TSV lanes, so open or resistive TSVs are decoded as erasures in the base die instead of being steered to spare TSVs by fuses after test.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): removes spare-TSV area and repair-fuse test steps and tolerates in-field TSV failures; targets several points of stack yield and lower test cost.

title: Bit-plane-transposed tensors: exponent planes refreshed, mantissa planes left drifting
idea: Combine approximate computing with bit-plane storage: the controller transposes BF16/FP8 tensors so each DRAM row holds one bit-plane; sign/exponent planes go to normally refreshed rows and low-mantissa planes to rows refreshed 8-16x less often, so any flip lands at a known, low significance.
why: Refresh cost (fact 3): AI tensors fill most HBM; cutting refresh on ~50-60% of bits saves ~5-10% DRAM power/bandwidth and lets weak-retention dies be sold into AI.

title: Low-distortion codes: weights stored so any bit flip barely matters
idea: Combine source coding with error tolerance: each 8-bit quantized weight is mapped to a 10-bit codeword chosen by a Gray/lattice-style assignment so that any single flip moves the decoded value by at most one quantization step; the code itself, not an ECC decoder, absorbs weak-cell errors with zero decode latency.
why: Weak cells for AI (facts 1, 3): allows raw BER ~1e-4 storage with no ECC engine, enabling relaxed refresh or lower-Cs cells for inference memory at 25% overhead.

title: Refresh-as-migration: Feistel row remapping advanced by refresh copies
idea: Combine refresh with RowClone-style in-subarray copy: each refresh step copies one row into a spare slot and advances a keyed Feistel permutation of logical-to-physical rows, so physical neighbors of any logical row change every few milliseconds and hammering cannot stay on fixed victims; the copy replaces the plain refresh.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations (fact 9): bounds per-victim disturbance without per-row counters, saving periphery SRAM/CAM area (fact 7).

title: Wi-Fi link adaptation for memory: per-page adaptive code rate
idea: Combine wireless adaptive modulation-and-coding with ECC: the controller tracks corrected-error counts per page and picks among 3-4 code strengths (SEC-DED, BCH-2, RS-4) the way Wi-Fi picks an MCS, storing the code ID in the page table, so parity concentrates where cells are weak.
why: Variability and retention tail (fact 3): average ECC overhead stays ~6% while weak regions get ~4x correction, letting dies with 10-100x higher raw BER ship.

title: Dedup-as-redundancy: duplicate pages become free mirrors for weak rows
idea: Combine page deduplication with mirroring: when the hypervisor finds identical pages it keeps two copies in different banks only if one sits on weak cells, using the twin as a recovery mirror; all other duplicates are merged, so net memory still shrinks.
why: Retention tail (fact 3) and supply: reuses the 10-30% natural duplication in VM/AI fleets as free redundancy, letting weak rows hold data without extra parity.

title: Checkpoint-replay memory: training runs on lightly refreshed DRAM
idea: Combine HPC checkpoint/restart with relaxed refresh: activations and optimizer state live in DRAM refreshed at 4-8x the nominal interval, and any ECC-detected failure triggers recomputation of the affected micro-batch from the last checkpoint, which training stacks already do for node failures.
why: Refresh energy/bandwidth (fact 3): recovers ~10-20% bandwidth and much of the 16-33% idle refresh power on training clusters and turns retention-marginal dies into usable supply.

title: One codeword from CPU core to capacitor: fused link-storage ECC
idea: Combine link CRC/retry with on-die and rank ECC into one end-to-end Reed-Solomon codeword generated in the CPU, carried unchanged over the bus and stored as-is; the DRAM die drops its own ECC engine and the module drops separate ECC chips, while the host decoder corrects both channel and cell errors.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7) and cost: removes duplicated on-die ECC logic and parity (~6% of die) plus x4 ECC devices while giving weaker cells stronger protection.

title: HBM base-die SRAM patch cache retires failing rows at runtime
idea: Combine a CPU victim cache with post-package repair: a small CAM+SRAM in the HBM logic die intercepts addresses of rows that start failing in the field and serves them from SRAM, removing fused spare rows from each DRAM die and allowing unlimited, reversible repairs.
why: Self-healing and yield (facts 6, 7): moves redundancy from 8-16 DRAM dies into one logic die on cheaper logic area, extending stack life and accepting dies with more defects.

title: Leak-direction-aware inversion: store each row mostly in safe state
idea: Combine data-bus inversion with the physics that true cells only leak 1->0: the controller inverts any row segment holding more charged than discharged cells and stores a flag bit, so at most half the cells sit in the vulnerable charged state; anti-cell regions use the opposite polarity.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): cuts the number of leakage-exposed cells ~30-50%, lowering retention errors and permitting longer refresh at ~1.5% overhead.

title: B-grade DRAM tier: buy JEDEC rejects, run them at 4x refresh
idea: Combine die binning with hyperscaler memory tiering: dies failing 64 ms retention but passing 16 ms are sold at a discount on modules whose controller profile sets 4x refresh and stronger ECC, deployed as a capacity tier for caching and inference KV-cache.
why: Usable supply and cost/bit: recovers a few percent of wafer output now scrapped or down-binned, at a tolerable bandwidth loss in capacity-bound tiers.

title: Decommissioned-server DRAM recertified by in-system retention retest
idea: Combine e-waste recycling with in-system profiling: retired DDR4/DDR5 modules pass through an automated rack that runs retention and hammer profiling, writes per-module weak-row maps into SPD and redeploys them behind stronger controller ECC as CXL-attached expansion.
why: Supply shortage: reclaims existing bits with no fab capital and US-located refurbishment, delivering usable memory at a fraction of new price.

title: Actuarial memory: price DRAM capacity by insured error budget
idea: Combine insurance actuarial models with ECC tiering: cloud providers sell memory at certified uncorrectable-error rates (e.g., 1e-17 vs 1e-14 per bit-hour) based on measured fleet data, with an insurance pool paying out on rare failures, so cheap weak-cell capacity is sold wherever the priced risk is acceptable.
why: Creates demand and a price signal for weaker, cheaper dies, enlarging usable supply; turns reliability margin into a priced product rather than a fixed spec.

title: Thermoelectric-cooled HBM stacks traded for 4x longer refresh
idea: Combine an in-package Peltier stage between GPU and HBM stack with temperature-indexed refresh: holding the DRAM ~20 C cooler roughly quadruples retention (leakage roughly doubles per ~10 C), so the refresh interval stretches and weak cells pass.
why: Refresh costs 16-33% of idle power and 10-20% of bandwidth (fact 3): recovers most of it in hot AI packages; Peltier power offsets part of the energy, but bandwidth gain is net.

title: Flash-style detrap pulses heal variable-retention-time cells in field
idea: Combine NAND erase-style detrapping with DRAM self-refresh: during idle, access transistors get brief negative-gate and reverse-junction bias pulses that empty the oxide/junction traps behind random-telegraph leakage, pushing VRT cells back into their low-leak state.
why: Leakage tail <=13 fA (fact 3): VRT cells force pessimistic refresh; pinning them low-leak could allow ~2x longer refresh and fewer field failures.

title: Diversity-pair cell: two capacitors with uncorrelated leakage physics
idea: Combine N-version design diversity with the cell: each bit is held by a silicon-access cell plus an oxide-semiconductor-access cell stacked above it, whose dominant leakage paths (junction GIDL vs. oxide trap-assisted) are uncorrelated; the pair is read as a charge sum, so a tail event in one device rarely coincides with one in the other.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): the product of two independent tail probabilities shrinks the refresh-limiting tail by orders of magnitude, enabling ~10x longer refresh; stacking offsets area.

title: SPD-embedded factory retention maps standardized through JEDEC
idea: Combine wafer-level test data with the module SPD: a policy push for a JEDEC field carrying per-bank/per-row retention bins measured at test, so every controller can apply multi-rate refresh and weak-row placement from day one without slow in-field profiling.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): multi-rate refresh can cut refresh operations ~70% but needs maps; standardization unlocks it industry-wide at near-zero cost.

title: Speculative early data return with late strong ECC verdict
idea: Combine CPU branch speculation with ECC: the controller forwards raw data immediately while a strong multi-symbol decoder runs in parallel; on an error the core squashes dependent instructions like a mispredicted branch and replays with corrected data.
why: Makes heavy ECC (needed for weak or low-Cs cells, fact 1) latency-free on the common path, permitting 10-100x higher raw BER without adding 5-15 ns decode latency.

title: Self-clearing capacitor electrodes borrowed from metallized-film power capacitors
idea: Combine the self-healing of metallized-film capacitors with DRAM MIM capacitors: an ALD ZrO2/Al2O3 dielectric under a 5-10 nm sputtered Al (or TiN/Al) top electrode thin enough that a breakdown spot's discharge vaporizes or oxidizes the electrode locally, isolating the defect while the cell keeps working at slightly lower C. Buildable in a university nanofab: ALD, sputter and lift-off only.
why: Dielectric weak-spot leakage and yield: converts leaky or shorted cells into working ones, permitting thinner, higher-C dielectrics (fact 1) with fewer failures.

title: Leaky-bucket hammer counter: IGZO TFT integrator on each wordline
idea: Combine the networking leaky-bucket with the wordline driver: each activation pumps a fixed charge quantum through an IGZO TFT onto a small MIM capacitor, while a subthreshold TFT drains it with a ~32-64 ms time constant; crossing a threshold triggers neighbor refresh. Buildable in a university nanofab: sputtered IGZO, ALD gate oxide and MIM at <=350 C.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): replaces per-row SRAM counters/CAMs in the periphery (fact 7) with an analog device whose decay matches the refresh window, at near-zero storage cost.

title: Wordline doubles as heater for periodic in-situ trap annealing
idea: Combine Joule microheaters with the array wordlines: in maintenance windows, after data is moved to another subarray, current through Mo or TiN wordline segments heats the local array to ~200-300 C for microseconds to milliseconds, annealing hydrogen-related and interface traps that create leakage tails. Buildable in a university nanofab: patterned Mo/TiN lines over IGZO or Si TFT arrays.
why: Retention tail and aging (fact 3): lifetime self-healing could tighten the tail 2-5x; also avoids tungsten wordlines (China ~80% chokepoint).

title: Three-tier charge-summing majority vote on a shared vertical bitline
idea: Combine triple modular redundancy with charge sharing: three cheap stacked oxide-TFT/capacitor tiers on one vertical bitline are written together and read by opening all three gates at once, so the bitline sees the analog sum and one fully leaked or shorted cell cannot flip the bit. Buildable in a university nanofab: three sequential low-temperature IGZO/MIM tiers.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): makes low-yield, leaky tiers acceptable because each bit tolerates a bad tier, enabling cheap BEOL stacking despite 3x cells.

title: Self-referencing rows: decaying reference cells set the read threshold
idea: Combine reference cells with the data row: each row carries a '1' and a '0' reference cell written with the data, so they decay alongside it; the sense threshold is set at the midpoint of their residual levels, letting partially leaked data resolve correctly. Buildable in a university nanofab: TFT/MIM test arrays with an off-chip comparator.
why: Retention (fact 3): reads tolerate ~2x more charge loss, allowing ~2x longer refresh or smaller Cs, robust to temperature swings.

title: NEMS relay access switch: air-gap off-state ends leakage tail
idea: Combine a nanoelectromechanical relay with a storage capacitor: a released TiN or poly-Si seesaw relay replaces the access transistor, so the off-state is an air gap with essentially zero leakage and retention is limited only by the capacitor dielectric. Buildable in a university nanofab: sacrificial oxide released by vapor HF, e-beam defined gaps.
why: Access-transistor leakage tail (fact 3): could stretch retention to minutes and remove most refresh; risk is contact endurance (~1e15 cycles needed) and switching speed.

title: 2D-heterojunction tunnel-diode pair makes a self-holding capacitor cell
idea: Combine Esaki tunnel-diode bistability (the 1990s TSRAM concept) with van der Waals heterojunctions: two series BP/MoS2 or WSe2/SnSe2 negative-differential-resistance diodes latch the storage node at one of two stable points with picoamp standby current, so the cell needs no refresh. Buildable in a university nanofab: flake transfer plus e-beam patterning.
why: Eliminates refresh energy and retention tail (fact 3) in a DRAM-like cell; risks are peak-to-valley ratio and uniformity.

title: Solar-cell recombination layer between cells absorbs hammer electrons
idea: Combine the defect-rich recombination junctions of tandem solar cells with DRAM isolation: line the gap between adjacent storage nodes with a thin, deliberately defective a-Si or heavily doped poly film that recombines electrons injected from the hammered row before they reach the victim node. Buildable in a university nanofab: PECVD/LPCVD film on paired-node test structures.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): attacks the charge-migration mechanism directly, potentially raising the flip threshold ~10x with no controller logic.

title: Sacrificial-polymer air gaps between wordlines cut hammer coupling
idea: Combine BEOL air-gap interconnect with DRAM wordlines: fill wordline gaps with a thermally decomposable polymer (polynorbornene or polycarbonate), cap with PECVD oxide and bake so the polymer diffuses out, leaving air gaps that cut line-to-line capacitance ~50%. Buildable in a university nanofab: spin-coat, PECVD and bake.
why: Row hammer and wordline energy (facts 9, 10): reduces capacitive disturbance coupled into neighbor rows and CV^2 wordline energy.

title: ReRAM soft-fuse table in BEOL enables lifelong self-repair
idea: Combine filamentary ReRAM (sputtered TaOx/HfOx between TiN electrodes) with the redundancy fuse bank: repair addresses live in a reprogrammable BEOL ReRAM array above the periphery, so the chip remaps newly failing rows in the field and can undo mistakes, replacing one-time laser/e-fuses. Buildable in a university nanofab: sputter plus two lithography layers.
why: Self-healing and periphery area (facts 3, 7): lifetime repairs cut field failure rates and free fuse area.

title: Inkjet-printed oxide memory made usable by heavy LDPC coding
idea: Combine solution-processed, inkjet-printed In-Zn-O TFT plus capacitor arrays (maskless, <300 C) with strong LDPC and spare-block mapping, so arrays with 1e-3 defect/BER rates still deliver error-free storage. Buildable in a university nanofab: a printer, hotplate and probe station.
why: Capital intensity and EUV (fact 4): tool cost drops by orders of magnitude; density is far lower, so it targets cheap capacity tiers and proves defect-tolerant design.

title: Test-then-write: maskless e-beam final metal routes around defects
idea: Combine wafer test with maskless lithography: after electrical test of the cell array, a per-die e-beam (or laser direct-write) exposure of the final metal layer is computed so bitline/wordline straps bypass defective cells and segments, giving every die custom wiring. Buildable in a university nanofab: e-beam writer plus probe-station test.
why: Yield and redundancy area (facts 4, 7): replaces built-in spare rows and fuses with per-die wiring; with multi-beam writers in production it raises yield of immature 3D or new-material arrays.

title: Dual-mode HZO/ZrO2 capacitor: volatile bit with ferroelectric safety copy
idea: Combine a DRAM capacitor with a ferroelectric backup in one ALD stack: a paraelectric ZrO2 layer holds the normal volatile charge, while a thin Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 layer is polarized only by an occasional higher-voltage backup pulse; if charge decays or ECC flags the row, the FE polarization is read to restore it. Buildable in a university nanofab: ALD plus <=400 C anneal.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): enables very long refresh intervals with FE as fallback, while rare switching limits FE fatigue.

title: Kelvin-probe imaging maps thousands of cell retention curves in parallel
idea: Combine Kelvin probe force microscopy with retention testing: fabricate arrays with exposed storage-node pads, write them, then time-lapse map surface potential across thousands of nodes to extract full leakage distributions and the spatial correlation of tail cells without per-cell probing. Buildable in a university nanofab: standard AFM/KPFM tool.
why: Retention-tail learning loop (fact 3): makes 1e-4 to 1e-6 tail statistics affordable for new-material cells, speeding tail-reduction R&D.

title: Hydrogen-getter cap layer stabilizes oxide-channel access transistor tails
idea: Combine Ti/Pd hydrogen-getter films from vacuum packaging with oxide-semiconductor access transistors: a patterned getter layer above the passivation absorbs mobile hydrogen that would otherwise drift into the channel and shift threshold voltage, narrowing the leakage and drift tail. Buildable in a university nanofab: sputtered metal and one lithography step.
why: Leakage tail and drift (fact 3): a tighter Vth distribution lowers the off-current tail and permits longer refresh.

title: Noise-cancelling wordlines: opposite pulses neutralize neighbor disturbance
idea: Combine active noise cancellation with wordline drive: when a wordline rises, drivers inject a small, timed opposite-polarity pulse on its two neighbors, cancelling the capacitively coupled disturbance on victim access gates; amplitude is calibrated per array. Buildable in a university nanofab: TFT arrays driven by external pulse generators.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): reduces coupling-driven victim leakage, potentially raising the flip threshold several-fold without counters.

title: Canary patch with thinned dielectric acts as self-timed refresh clock
idea: Combine canary cells with an oscillator: each subarray holds a few cells with a deliberately leakier, thinner dielectric patch, and their decay crossing triggers that subarray's refresh, automatically tracking temperature, aging and process instead of a fixed worst-case timer. Buildable in a university nanofab: one extra lithography step and a thinner ALD deposition.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): replaces one worst-case interval with locally tracked ones, cutting refresh ~2-4x at moderate temperatures.

title: Open-PDK shuttle CMOS plus university BEOL cell post-processing
idea: Combine open-source SKY130/GF180 shuttle chips carrying sense amps, ECC and refresh controllers with university post-processing of capacitor or oxide-TFT arrays on the top-metal pads, giving full-stack reliability testbeds (real arrays plus real ECC) for a few tens of thousands of dollars. Buildable in a university nanofab: low-temperature BEOL steps on diced shuttle die.
why: Speeds iteration on reliability schemes for new cells (facts 2, 3) and builds US memory know-how; a strategy rather than a cell.

title: Dielectric-absorption reservoir: slow polarization refills leaking storage node
idea: Combine dielectric absorption (soakage, normally a capacitor flaw) with DRAM: a bilayer of fast linear dielectric plus a slow-relaxing defect-dipole layer (Nb- or La-doped ZrO2) releases polarization charge back onto the node over milliseconds after a write, offsetting junction leakage and flattening the decay curve. Buildable in a university nanofab: ALD doping supercycles.
why: Charge wall and retention (facts 1, 3): adds effective storage at long timescales without fast capacitance; speculative ~2x retention.

title: Laser-trim healing: test, then locally anneal each leaky cell
idea: Combine laser trimming of analog resistors with retention test: after mapping tail cells, a focused laser pulse locally anneals each leaky cell's junction or channel to passivate the defect, or deliberately opens it so it is mapped out. Buildable in a university nanofab: laser writer plus probe-station retention map.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): targeted repair of the ~1e-5 tail could double the refresh interval; production needs fast galvo systems.

title: Solar-cell Al2O3 field-effect passivation lines storage-node isolation
idea: Combine the negative fixed charge of ALD Al2O3 (used to passivate PERC solar cells) with DRAM isolation: line storage-node trenches with ALD Al2O3 so its built-in charge repels electrons from surfaces, suppressing surface-generation leakage and electron migration from aggressor rows. Buildable in a university nanofab: one ALD step and forming-gas anneal.
why: Retention tail and row hammer (facts 3, 9): field-effect passivation cuts surface generation currents by up to ~10x.

title: Self-restoring gain cell: one global pulse refreshes whole array
idea: Combine a gain cell with bootstrapped positive feedback: each 2T IGZO cell's storage node gates a second TFT that connects a pulsed restore rail back to the node, so pulsing the rail tops up only cells storing '1' (cells at '0' keep it off), refreshing the whole array in one pulse with no row activation or sensing. Buildable in a university nanofab: two-mask n-type IGZO TFT process.
why: Refresh bandwidth and energy (fact 3): removes the 10-20% bandwidth loss and per-row activation energy of refresh; risk is threshold loss needing a boosted rail.

title: Plate-line popcount probe checks row health without activating it
idea: Combine popcount checksums with segmented plate-line charge sensing: pulsing a row segment's plate and integrating the displaced charge gives its total stored charge (about the count of '1's); comparing it with a stored popcount detects leakage or hammer flips non-destructively, so only drifted rows are refreshed or scrubbed. Buildable in a university nanofab: segmented-plate MIM arrays with an off-chip integrator.
why: Destructive read and refresh (facts 3, 8, 9): refreshing only drifted rows could cut refresh activations >5x.
